title: New Center framework turns sustainability risk into a decision-making tool
summary: A new "sustainability framework" from The Center proposes to help shipping lines de-risk future fuel investments beyond basic carbon metrics. This initiative prioritizes corporate reputation and long-term financial exposure, rather than immediate, verifiable reductions in HFO consumption or carbon intensity. Until tangible cuts in CO2 emissions are demonstrated and FuelEU Maritime compliance is met, such frameworks risk becoming another layer of greenwashing.
content:
For years, decarbonization decisions centered on two questions: is it technically feasible, and is it economically viable? Today, a third question is becoming just as important: is it sustainable beyond the carbon?

Sustainability isn’t only about reducing greenhouse gas emissions. As shipping moves towards a multi-fuel future, each fuel choice carries its own risks: resource availability, shifting regulations, reputational exposure, and pressure from stakeholders.

A fuel that works at pilot scale, in one region, under one regulatory regime, may not hold as it scales.

Left unmanaged, these risks can undermine even a long-term decarbonization strategy with solid technical and economic foundations.

The risks you don’t see coming

Many sustainability risks sit upstream in a fuel’s value chain: in feedstock production, energy sourcing, land use, and third-party certification integrity. Companies buying the fuel have little direct control, but they can still be held accountable when something goes wrong.

Without early visibility, a company can lock into a fuel pathway that later proves reputationally, socially, or commercially indefensible. A fuel can pass every test on cost and feasibility and still carry very different risks depending on its origin and supplier.

By surfacing these risks before capital is committed, the Center’s Sustainability Framework can help companies decide which low-emissions fuels to invest in.

As sustainability requirements across shipping tighten, from fuel certification to emissions accounting, early assessment of which fuel pathways will remain compliant let companies secure long-term supply with confidence.

Introducing the Center’s Sustainability Framework

The framework is built on earth system science, the Center’s understanding of a just and equitable transition, and a holistic approach to decarbonization that looks beyond carbon alone. It translates planetary boundaries and social and socioeconomic criteria based on recent discussion at the IMO into 14 practical sustainability dimensions, grouped as:

Importantly, these sustainability dimensions are interrelated. A fuel that cuts emissions can increase pressure on land or water, while another can deliver benefits well beyond carbon. The framework maps these connections across the whole value chain, so leadership teams can compare options and see trade-offs before their fuel choices are locked in.

In practice, the framework delivers three things:

• The right conversation: Sustainability, procurement, and strategy teams work from the same picture. The framework enables informed discussions of synergies and trade-offs and supports decisions based on a shared understanding.

• Synergies as well as risks: Decarbonization investments often bring co-benefits that go unrecorded, from local jobs to improved land management. The framework brings these into view, so the business case reflects the full value of a decision.

• Levers for action: The framework helps identify trade-offs and highlights where they can be addressed or mitigated along the value chain. It also supports the definition of minimum sustainability thresholds when assessing suppliers.

The Sustainability Framework in practice

Together with our strategic partner Hapag-Lloyd and its decarbonization team, we ran five real-world fuel pathways through the Sustainability Framework:

• Ammonia

• Biomethane

• Cashew nutshell liquid (CNSL)

• Fatty acid methyl esters (FAME, also known as biodiesel)

• Very low-sulfur fuel oil (VLSFO)

Each fuel was assessed across the same sustainability dimensions, giving Hapag-Lloyd a single, comparable view of risk across fundamentally different fuel types. As the potential fuel buyer, Hapag-Lloyd provided data on current and potential suppliers and led the assessment of the available fuel options. The Center supported the analysis by providing the assessment framework and LCA expertise, including a high-level review of the risks associated with each fuel.

With line of sight across the value chain, the buyer can select the best-positioned supplier for each fuel pathway. Factors like how a supplier sources feedstock, manages land and water use, and treats the communities and workers in its value chain sit alongside price and volume.

When we took a closer look at FAME, at first glance all the assessed suppliers looked equally strong on emissions reductions. But the framework made it visible that one supplier’s feedstock carried substantial food security and freshwater risks, while the others’ did not. Same fuel, very different exposure.

Arne Maibohm, Director Decarbonization, Hapag-Lloyd AG

The view from Hapag-Lloyd

Hapag-Lloyd’s sustainability team found the framework highly useful, supporting the assessment of future fuels while also prompting a reassessment of fuels already in use, looking beyond carbon intensity alone.

The framework enhanced the questions we must ask, not only about the fuels we plan to use, but about the ones we use today. Better data will be available as the industry matures, and the companies that start enhancing their questions now will be the ones best prepared for it.

Choosing the right fuel is no longer only about carbon. It is about better understanding all elements of sustainability in the full value chain behind the fuel. The framework gave us that perspective and showed that transparency is something the whole industry has to build together, with suppliers as partners.

Arne Maibohm, Director Decarbonization, Hapag-Lloyd AG

Three lessons learned from the framework pilot

Data input

Supplier sustainability certificates are the most reliable source today, but they mostly cover carbon intensity. For the other dimensions, future users should expect to rely on estimates from life-cycle studies and academic research, with differing units and boundaries. Social risks, assessed by reviewing media coverage for controversies, proved easier to quantify than expected.

Visualization

With reliable data, results are simple to visualize. The team is now evaluating where to set the thresholds for each risk level.

Communication with external parties

Responses are often slow and incomplete, given the complexity of supply chains and the many traders between producer and buyer. Short, precise questions work best to obtain a direct answer, and stricter requirements can be set for new suppliers.

As the industry matures, the Hapag-Lloyd sustainability team expects data transparency to improve. Until then, working with the Center makes the difference: the method, the reference data, and the experience of a first full pilot.

Next steps: rolling out the framework to new users

The Hapag-Lloyd pilot is the first in a series. The Center is now opening the Sustainability Framework and its underlying model to the wider maritime industry. With tools like this framework, sustainability risk can move from a niche concern to a standard part of how the sector makes decarbonization decisions.
